title: The Qal yiqtol

objectives.can: Recognise a Qal yiqtol form and give its person, gender and number.

explanation.summary: The yiqtol is the Hebrew verb form that marks the person with a prefix on the front of the stem, and sometimes with an ending as well. It presents an action as not yet complete, so it is used for what will happen, what usually happens, what may or must happen. It is not simply 'the future tense'.

sections.heading: A prefix tells you the person
body: The qatal you have met builds its forms by adding endings to the stem. The yiqtol works the other way round: a prefix comes first, and the prefix names the person. The consonants are י for the third person, ת for the second person (and for the third feminine singular), א for 'I' and נ for 'we'. The traditional name for this form is the 'imperfect', and the modern name 'yiqtol' is simply the shape of the third masculine singular of a model root.

For the plural, and for the feminine singular of the second person, an ending is added after the stem: -וּ for the masculine plural, -ִי for the second feminine singular, -נָה for the feminine plural. Because the ending names the gender and number and the prefix names the person, the two together give you the full parse.

A prefix on the verb is easy to confuse with a word-initial prefix such as ו, 'and', or ה, the question particle. Those come before the yiqtol prefix: in the word וְאֶשְׁמְרָה the ו is 'and' and the א is 'I'. The word-by-word display shows such particles as the feature Prefix and keeps them apart from the person prefix.

sections.heading: The stem vowel and the shape of the word
body: The stem of a strong Qal yiqtol is built on its root consonants with the prefix and a vowel between the second and third root letters. In most strong verbs that vowel is ō (holem), as in the yiqtol of שָׁמַר 'keep', and the first root letter has no vowel of its own. In a number of verbs the vowel is a (patah) instead; this happens often when the last root letter is a guttural, as with שָׁמַע 'hear', but it is not a rule that you can predict from the letters alone. Learn the vowel with the verb, as a dictionary does.

When an ending beginning with a vowel is added (-וּ, -ִי), the stem vowel is reduced to a shewa or lost, and the stress moves onto the ending. So the third masculine singular and the third masculine plural look quite different at the end of the word. Watch the endings first and the vowels second.

The paradigm below is built from the verses of the Bible by the lesson, not typed by hand. A dash in a cell means that the form does not happen to occur in the texts, not that it cannot exist. The second and third persons are shown in the masculine; the third feminine singular has the shape of the second masculine singular (see below). First-person forms have no gender: the same form serves a man or a woman speaking.

sections.heading: Two forms that are written alike
body: The third feminine singular and the second masculine singular have exactly the same shape: both begin with ת and both have the bare stem. A form such as תִּשְׁמֹר can be 'she will keep' or 'you (masculine) will keep'. Nothing in the word tells you which. The context does: the subject of the sentence, or the person addressed, decides. In Genesis 17:9 the verb is plainly addressed to Abraham ('you'); in Genesis 21:12 the subject is Sarah ('she').
In the same way the second and third feminine plural are identical. The texts have few of these forms, so you will meet the rule more often in the grammars than in the verses.

sections.heading: What the yiqtol does
body: A grammarian, S. R. Driver, described the yiqtol as presenting an action as incomplete, in progress or still to come, without placing it at any particular point in time. That is a useful starting point but it is one scholar's description, and Hebrew scholars still discuss how best to put it. What can be said for certain is that the yiqtol is used in several ways, and the context chooses among them.

It is often future: 'you shall surely die'. It is often habitual or general: 'a man leaves his father and his mother'. It can express what is permitted or what is commanded, as in 'from every tree of the garden you may eat' or, with a negative, 'you shall not murder'. It can express what is possible or desired. It can also refer to a past habit. English has no single tense that does all this, so do not translate the yiqtol with 'will' every time.

misunderstandings: The yiqtol is not 'the future tense'. It is often used of the future, but it is also the form of habits, general truths, permissions and commands. Read the sentence round it.
A ת at the front does not always mean 'you'. It also begins the third feminine singular, and the third feminine plural. Check the subject.

A word that begins with וַ and then looks like a yiqtol, as וַיִּשְׁמֹר does, is not an ordinary yiqtol. It is the narrative form called the wayyiqtol, taught later. A plain וְ or וּ in front of a yiqtol is just 'and'.
The prefix does not show the root. The first root letter of a strong verb comes after the prefix, but weak roots lose or change their letters, which later lessons teach.

deeper.heading: The same prefixes in other languages
body: A prefix conjugation that marks person at the front of the verb, with t- for the second person and n- for 'we', is found across the Semitic languages; Arabic, Ethiopic and Akkadian have comparable forms. This is one of the signs that these languages are related. In Hebrew itself the same prefix shapes are used for the jussive and the cohortative, which will appear in a later lesson.

examples.analysis: תֹאכַל is a Qal yiqtol of אָכַל, second masculine singular: God is speaking to the man. With לֹא it gives a prohibition, 'you shall not eat'. The last word, תָּמוּת, is the yiqtol of מוּת, also second masculine singular, preceded by its own infinitive (a later lesson). Both are about what lies ahead, but the first is an instruction and the second a consequence.
